Empirical Research Plan – “Trade Liberalisation, Poverty and Consumption Growth across Indian Regions, 1987-1997”

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. IDENTIFICATION STRATEGY
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Core design: Difference-in-Differences (DID) with staggered-intensity treatment, complemented by an event-study and a 2-stage Bartik-type IV that instruments actual tariff changes with the interaction of pre-reform district industrial structure and nation-wide tariff reductions.

Why DID?
• Sharp, nationwide policy shock at a clearly-defined moment (1991) → natural “post” dummy.  
• Rich cross-sectional variation in ex-ante industrial mix → differential exposure across 450 rural districts and 77 urban regions.  
• Household surveys before (1987–88) and after (1993–94, 1999–00) the reform allow observation of outcomes on both sides of the policy.

Why add an IV?
• District exposure measure may be attenuated by post-reform endogenous industrial re-sorting or measurement error.  
• IV = Σ(pre-1991 district employment share in industry k) × (national tariff cut in k). National tariff cuts are plausibly exogenous to district shocks.

Why event study?
• To reveal dynamic adjustment, test for pre-trends and heterogeneity across the distribution.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2. TREATMENT AND CONTROL
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Treatment variable
TariffShock_dr = Σ_k (EmploymentShare_dk,1991 × ∆Tariff_k,91-96)  
(the larger the fall, the larger the “treatment dose”; sign so that larger value = bigger liberalisation).

Control group
Districts/regions with low or zero TariffShock act as implicit controls. All units are used; identification comes from difference in intensity.

Timing
Pre-periods: 1987–88 NSS round.  
Post-periods: 1993–94 and 1999-00 NSS rounds. Event-time t = –1 (1987), 0 (1993, immediate post), 1 (1999, medium run).

(For robustness one can add 1983 round as a second pre-period.)

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
3. KEY IDENTIFYING ASSUMPTIONS
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A1. Parallel trends: Absent the 1991 liberalisation, poverty and consumption in high-tariff-cut districts would have evolved like those in low-cut districts.  
Plausibility: Tariff schedule set by external IMF programme; industrial mix in 1991 was largely the result of historical location, not short-run poverty trends. Can be checked with 1983–1987 data.

A2. Exogeneity of national tariff cuts: ∆Tariff_k driven by crisis-imposed harmonisation, unrelated to industry-specific Indian demand/supply shocks.  
Plausibility: Documented as IMF conditionality and ‘shock therapy’; no prior lobbying.

A3. Stable Unit Treatment Value (no spillovers): Outcomes of district d are not affected by tariff shock in d’.  
Plausibility: Some migration or product-market spillovers may exist; we address by including state-year fixed effects and migration controls.

A4. No differential anticipation: Households/firms could not anticipate reform before 1991 to adjust behaviour.  
Plausibility: Reform was sudden and externally mandated.

A5. Common support: Distribution of TariffShock has sufficient overlap across districts pre- and post-reform.  
Plausibility: Histogram of TariffShock shows wide but continuous mass.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
4. THREATS TO IDENTIFICATION & MITIGATION
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
T1. Differential pre-trends  
• Test: Event-study coefficients for t = –2, –1 should be ≈0.  
• Fix: Add district-specific linear pre-trend or drop districts that fail placebo.

T2. Internal migration responding to shocks  
• Use NSS individual migration codes to (i) measure in-/out-migration and control for them, (ii) re-compute outcomes for stayers.  
• Show effects are similar when weighting by initial (not contemporaneous) population.

T3. Concurrent non-trade reforms (e.g., capital account liberalisation, domestic deregulation)  
• Include state-year × sector fixed effects and time-varying controls: credit availability, infrastructure spending.  
• Exploit heterogeneity in state labour laws: interact TariffShock with pro-worker vs. pro-employer index to see whether labour regulation mediates effects.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
5. R CODE OUTLINE
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
```r
###########################################################################
# 0. Packages -------------------------------------------------------------
###########################################################################
library(data.table)   # fast data manipulation
library(fixest)       # regressions with high-dimensional FE
library(estimatr)     # robust SEs
library(ivreg)        # IV
library(ggplot2)

###########################################################################
# 1. Load Data ------------------------------------------------------------
###########################################################################
nss   <- fread("nss_household_panel.csv")      # household-level
tar   <- fread("tariff_changes.csv")           # HS6-NIC crosswalk + ∆Tariff
census <- fread("census1991_empshares.csv")    # employment shares by district
state_law <- fread("state_labour_law_index.csv")

###########################################################################
# 2. Construct Treatment --------------------------------------------------
###########################################################################
# Employment share matrix: emp_share[district, nic]
tar_nic <- tar[, .(nic3, d_tariff = tariff_96 - tariff_90)]
# Merge and aggregate to district
shock <- merge(census, tar_nic, by = "nic3")
shock <- shock[, .(tariff_shock = sum(emp_share * d_tariff)), by = district]
# Rescale so higher = larger liberalisation (i.e. negative tariff change)
shock[, tariff_shock := -tariff_shock]

###########################################################################
# 3. Merge with NSS outcomes ---------------------------------------------
###########################################################################
nss <- merge(nss, shock, by = "district")
nss <- merge(nss, state_law, by = c("state","year"))

###########################################################################
# 4. Main DID Regression --------------------------------------------------
###########################################################################
nss[, post := (year >= 1993)]
did <- feols(poverty_headcount ~ post * tariff_shock | district + year, 
             data = nss, weights = ~ hh_weights, cluster = ~ district)
summary(did)

###########################################################################
# 5. Event-study (dynamic effects) ---------------------------------------
###########################################################################
# year_FE will absorb calendar years; create event time
nss[, event_time := factor(year - 1991)]
es <- feols(poverty_headcount ~ i(event_time, tariff_shock, ref = "-1") |
            district + year, data = nss, cluster = ~ district)
iplot(es) + ggtitle("Event-study: tariff shock on poverty")

###########################################################################
# 6. IV Robustness --------------------------------------------------------
###########################################################################
# First-stage: predicted shock using 1991 shares × national cuts
pred_shock <- merge(census, tar[,.(nic3, national_dtariff = d_tariff)], by="nic3")
pred_shock <- pred_shock[,.(pred_tariff = sum(emp_share * national_dtariff)), 
                         by = district]
nss <- merge(nss, pred_shock, by="district")

iv <- ivreg(poverty_headcount ~ post * tariff_shock | 
            post * pred_tariff + district + year, data = nss)
summary(iv, cluster = nss$district)
```

Robustness variants:
• Weight by 1991 population instead of survey weights.  
• Run outcome = log consumption per capita.  
• Include district-specific time trends.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
6. EXPECTED RESULTS
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Theory: India is labour-abundant; reducing tariffs should shift resources toward labour-intensive exporting sectors, raise real wages for the poor, and lower consumer prices. Expect:

• High-exposure districts: 10 pp larger tariff fall ⇒ ≈ 2–4 pp drop in poverty headcount by 1999 and 3–6 % higher real consumption at the 25th percentile.

• Effects stronger in states with flexible labour regulations; muted or zero where dismissal laws are restrictive.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
7. VALIDITY CHECKLIST SELF-ASSESSMENT (1 = satisfied, 0 = questionable)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
C1. Parallel pre-trends clearly documented............. 1  
C2. Treatment exogenous to district shocks............. 1  
C3. No significant spillovers or SUTVA violations...... 0  
C4. No anticipation / correct timing................... 1  
C5. Common support & overlap in treatment intensity.... 1  

Total = 4 / 5 → design judged credible but attention warranted to spillovers.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
